opening_summary: Thirty-four terms for a design that an engineer can build from and a tester can check, from its sections and tags to the ways it goes wrong. The exact terms let you tell an AI agent what to write.
opening_description: 34 GDD terms: sections, tags, tests, failure modes.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often treat a GDD, the game design document, as a story about the game. It is not. It is a promise that other people, and agents, can build from and check, with every claim tagged and every test linked. This film goes through its terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
A GDD is
a story about the game.
idea.replacementWords: a promise others can build and check

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-four terms about the GDD, the game design document, in four groups. A GDD is a promise that other people, and agents, can build from and check. The first group is the documents, the GDD, game brief, pitch, reverse, draft and gate.

The second group is what the design says. Sixteen sections, design pillar, core loop, PX goal, the player experience goal, mechanic, scope, out of scope, scope creep, and cut, defer, swap. These terms are what a GDD commits to.

The third group is linking and checking. Stable ID, a fixed identifier, and linked test, then the tags observed, inferred, missing and assumption, then acceptance criterion, given-when-then, tolerance, direct state write, invariant and false pass. These terms say how a claim points at its evidence.

The fourth group is seven ways a GDD goes wrong. Ghost Center, Mechanic Mirage, Implementation Void, Priority Inflation, Novelist's Trap, Completeness Fallacy and Stagnant Artifact. These are the failure modes a review looks for.

Three bars, drawn to length. The top one is the GDD. It says what the game is and how it plays, in enough detail that an engineer can build it and a tester can check it. This one is a real recovered GDD of four thousand seven hundred seventy-seven words. The brief agrees the task, and the GDD details it. For example, a GDD for your platformer gives the robot's jump height in metres, so a test can measure the jump.

The red bar is the Game brief. It says what the player does, what success is, what can go wrong, and what is left out. Its reader is the team, and its job is to agree the task and its limits. In this made-up example it runs to six hundred words. For example, a brief for a coin game says, collect every coin before time runs out, falling off the level loses, and multiplayer is out.

The short grey bar is the Pitch, a short sales description of the game idea. Its reader is someone you want to persuade, and it does not have to be buildable yet. Here the made-up pitch is one hundred fifty words, and the GDD is about thirty-two times as long. For example, a pitch for a robot platformer sells the thrill of the chase and the hunt for coins, and gives an engineer nothing to build yet.

A diagram of game files feeding into a GDD. Reverse means recovering a GDD from a game that already exists. The agent reads the scripts and scenes, and every claim it writes carries a tag that says how it is known. This real one has one hundred seven observed claims, twenty-nine inferred and thirty missing. For example, you point the agent at a finished platformer, and it records that falling off the level resets the player, citing the script line that does it.

Below it, an idea feeds into a GDD. Draft means writing a GDD from a new idea, with no files yet, and marking what you assumed. Every gap the agent fills in carries an assumption tag. Reverse starts from the game, draft starts from the idea, and both end in the same sixteen sections. For example, you describe a cave game that has no code yet, and every guessed number in the draft, such as the jump height, is tagged as an assumption.

The picture changes to four design phases, vision, systems, world and scope, with a gate after each. A Gate is a named sign-off after a design phase, and only a person signs it. In a silent run all four stay unsigned. When a person answers, they are signed in order, four of four. The agent asks, a person answers, the agent records. For example, after the agent drafts your game's vision, you look it over and sign the vision gate before systems work begins.

A four by four grid fills in, one tile at a time. The Sixteen sections are the fixed outline of a GDD, always in the same order, from metadata through pillars, core loop, mechanics and world, to risks and open questions. A tester can find any decision by its section. For example, to check how your robot's jump should work, a tester opens the mechanics section, and to see whether online play is planned, the out of scope section.

The Pillars tile is picked out. A Design pillar is a core principle that every decision must support. A GDD has only a few, and every later section is checked against them. A pillar guides choices, while the core loop is what the player repeats. For example, a platformer with the pillar, falling is never a harsh punishment, keeps respawns quick and drops any feature that would take away much of the player's progress.

Now the Core loop tile is lit. The Core loop is the repeated, moment-to-moment cycle the player enjoys, and everything else in the design hangs off it. It is an action the player repeats, not a principle. For example, in a coin platformer the loop is run, jump, grab a coin and run on, and a checkpoint exists to keep that loop going after a fall.

A graph begins with four goals on the left, control, reward, recovery and clarity, in this made-up example. A PX goal is a feeling the player should have, written in plain words and given an ID such as PX zero one. A PX goal is what the player should feel, and a mechanic is what the player can do. For example, the player feels safe to try a risky jump is a PX goal for a platformer.

Five mechanics join the goals. A Mechanic is a rule-governed action in the game, something the player can do that the rules decide. Each one should serve a goal, and here every goal has at least one. Jump and shoot both serve control. For example, a checkpoint pad that moves your respawn point when you stand on it is a mechanic, and it serves the goal of recovery.

Now every box carries a label, PX zero one to PX zero four, and M zero one to M zero five. A Stable ID is a label that never changes, so a ticket, a test and a playtest note all point at the same thing. For example, a playtest note says M zero two, coins hard to see, and the agent and the test both know it means the coin mechanic, even after the coins are renamed gems.

Six tests appear on the right, T twenty to T twenty-five. A Linked test is a test row that names the mechanic it checks. Follow the lines, and six tests cover four of the five mechanics. M zero three, shoot, has no test, and because each row names its mechanic, the gap shows. For example, one test row says, touch task B before task A, and the task ledger does not change, and it names M zero five, task order.

A bar of tagged claims from a real recovered GDD. The tag OBSERVED means the code does this, and the tag names the file and line that show it. Here one hundred seven of one hundred sixty-six claims, sixty-four percent, are observed. A tag is a claim, not evidence, so open the line. For example, a tag says the player respawns after falling off the level and cites a line of the player script, and you open that line to see the reset.

The middle grey part is INFERRED. The code strongly implies the claim without stating it, so the tag must give its evidence. Twenty-nine of the one hundred sixty-six claims, seventeen percent, are inferred. For example, coins placed in a trail along a ledge suggest the route the designer meant the player to take, and the GDD says so, with the coin positions as its evidence.

The light grey part is MISSING. It marks something the code cannot tell you, so nobody should guess it from the files. Thirty of the one hundred sixty-six claims, eighteen percent, are missing. For example, no script in a recovered platformer says who the target player is or how the game is won, so both are tagged missing, for a person to decide.

A second bar shows a draft, in this made-up example. ASSUMPTION marks a gap the draft filled in, which nobody saw in any code. Here it is twenty-six of fifty claims, fifty-two percent, the largest share and the one to watch. Observed means the code does it, and assumption means the draft guessed. For example, a draft for a new game gives its enemies a patrol speed, and that speed stays tagged as an assumption until a person decides it.

Two boxes of twelve dots each, from the same simulated draws. Ghost Center is the failure where no vision is locked, so nothing anchors the decisions and each one drifts. With no vision the dots miss the centre by one hundred thirty pixels on average, and with a locked vision by forty-one. For example, a team that never settles whether its game is a calm exploration or a speed run ends up with slow puzzles in one level and timed races in the next.

Now four PX goals are tested. A Mechanic Mirage is a PX goal that is really a feature described in disguise. Two of these, add a rope swing and build a skill tree, name features, not feelings, so nobody can tell when the goal is met. The test is whether you can say it without naming a feature. For example, add a double jump is a mirage, and the real goal might be, the player feels free in the air.

This list is the checkpoint pad, mechanic M zero four. An Implementation Void is a mechanic with only the happy path written down, the case where all goes right. At first only walk onto the pad is written. Then the unhappy cases fill in, walking on again, resets, a fall, and the old checks, until six of six are written. For example, a locked door that only says, the key opens it, is a void until it says what happens without the key.

Fifteen feature tiles, and eight turn red as they are tagged CORE, the tag for what the game cannot do without. Priority Inflation means more than forty percent of the features are tagged CORE. Eight of fifteen is fifty-three point three percent, over the line, and when most things are core, nothing is. For example, a platformer that tags hat skins, a photo mode and a leaderboard as core, beside run and jump, has inflated its priorities.

Two of the CORE tiles are demoted. Six of fifteen is exactly forty percent, which is not more than the limit, so it passes. This step is made-up arithmetic. Demoting is the fix for priority inflation, deciding that a feature can be cut or deferred. For example, demote the photo mode and the leaderboard to later, and keep run, jump and the checkpoint as core.

Two cards of sentences, made up for this example. The Novelist's Trap is story written for a reader, not for an engineer. The ruins sigh with old grief is pleasant, and nobody can build it. On the left one of three sentences is buildable, and on the right all three are. For example, your robot feels lonely in the dark caves gives an engineer nothing, while the cave lights dim as the robot goes deeper gives a lighting task.

A table of six decisions, made up for this example. The Completeness Fallacy is a GDD full of decisions with no recorded reasoning. It looks complete, yet only two of six decisions say why. Gravity twenty-two, with no reason, could be a choice or an accident. For example, if your GDD sets the jump height and never says why, a teammate may change it without knowing a level depends on it.

Two version timelines over ten weeks, in this made-up history, with a prototype built at week five. A Stagnant Artifact is a GDD with no version history, never revised after a prototype. The top one is revised three times after the prototype, the bottom one zero. For example, playtesting your prototype shows the checkpoints are too far apart, and a living GDD gets a new version that says so, while a stagnant one keeps the old plan.

A list of six items with their hours, in this made-up plan. Scope is everything the project promises to include. Here move and jump, coins, enemies, a checkpoint pad, three levels and a menu add up to ninety-four of one hundred hours. For example, if your scope promises three levels, those three are what you owe, and any extra level is new work that must be agreed first.

A red box adds the out-of-scope list. Out of scope is a written list of what will not be built, here multiplayer, a mobile port and XR, extended reality. It is excluded on purpose, so a request for multiplayer already has an answer. For example, a checkpoint pad's acceptance criterion lists its look and sound, touch, gamepad and any export as out of scope, so nobody expects them in that build.

Three red items slip in, an extra boss, skins and a day-night cycle. Scope creep is the quiet growth of work beyond what was agreed. Nobody decided to add these, and the total is now one hundred thirty of one hundred hours. Creep is growth nobody agreed to, and out of scope is excluded on purpose. For example, an agent asked to fix the jump also adds a wall climb, because it seemed nice, and nobody approved it.

Cut, defer, swap are the three ways to handle too much scope. Cut removes a thing, defer postpones it, and swap replaces it with something smaller. Here the skins are cut, the day-night cycle is deferred, and the boss becomes a six hour mini-boss, so the plan is back to one hundred of one hundred hours. For example, you cut an extra costume, defer online leaderboards until after launch, and swap a flying enemy for one that only walks.

Six checks for a checkpoint pad, with values measured in a real run. An Acceptance criterion is a concrete condition that must be true for work to count as done. A stranger could write its test without asking, from a quantity and unit, a limit, a time box and how the state is reached. Here six of six pass. For example, the robot should feel responsive is a wish, and the robot reaches the pad within six hundred frames is a criterion.

Check four, rewritten in three parts. Given-when-then is a format for a test, a starting state, an action and an expected result. Given the pad is active and the player stands elsewhere, when reset is held for five frames, then the player is within zero point two metres of the respawn point. It measured zero point zero eight eight two. For example, given the player stands by the last coin, when it is touched, then the goal door opens.

A top view of the zero point two metre limit. A Tolerance is the allowed difference between what you expected and what you got. The real result, zero point zero eight eight two metres, lands inside the ring and passes, and the made-up point at zero point three five fails. The time box counts engine frames, sixty-four of six hundred. For example, a test of where the robot lands after a jump accepts a small gap from the target, instead of an exact match.

A chart of player height by frame. A Direct state write sets a value in code instead of producing it through gameplay. The red line puts the player at minus thirteen metres at frame zero, skipping nine frames of falling, at a made-up fall speed. It tests what follows, not whether a player can get there. For example, a test that sets the score straight to the winning total checks the win screen, but not that the coins can be collected.

A list of five old checks. An Invariant is a condition that must stay true throughout, whatever else changes. Here movement, jump, a projectile, reset and a collected coin must all still pass after the checkpoint is added, and five of five still hold. A change that breaks one fails. For example, when an agent adds a dash move to your player, the invariant that the old jump test still passes must hold.

Twenty-one pass lines are printed, and two turn red. A False pass is a test that passes though the behaviour is wrong. Two of these were skips that still printed pass, so only nineteen of twenty-one tested anything. These counts are from a real test session. Weakening a check so it passes is called loosening. For example, a coin test that cannot find the coin, skips itself and prints pass, proves nothing about coins.

Each pair sets look-alike terms side by side. Reverse starts from a game that exists, and most of its claims are tagged observed. Draft starts from an idea, and tags its guesses as assumptions. Both arrows end in a GDD.

A Brief is short, about six hundred words in the made-up case, and agrees the task, success and limits. A GDD is long, a real four thousand seven hundred seventy-seven words, detailed enough to build and test.

OBSERVED means the code does it, and a file and line show it, here line thirty-six of the player script, falls below minus twelve. ASSUMPTION is a gap the draft filled in, with no file, no line, only a question mark.
A Mechanic is what the player can do, such as jump or shoot, an action. A PX goal is what the player should feel, such as feeling in control, an experience. Each mechanic should serve a goal.

A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it, with a chart of what it does. Make the GDD complete becomes, fill all sixteen sections and tag every claim, observed, inferred, missing or assumption. Then every one of one hundred sixty-six claims has a tag.
Do not make everything a priority becomes, tag no more than forty percent of features CORE, at most six of fifteen. Before, fifty-three percent. After demoting two, forty.

The checkpoint should respond well becomes, return the player within zero point two metres of the respawn point within two frames, at a fixed sixty frames per second. Measured in a constructed fixture that sets the player below the fall threshold in code, not by play, zero point zero eight nine eight metres, under the limit.
Say what we are not doing becomes, write an out-of-scope list, then cut, defer or swap until the plan fits one hundred hours. With creep it was one hundred thirty, so thirty hours come out.
Make sure every mechanic is tested becomes, give each test an ID and name its mechanic, and list any mechanic with no test. Six tests, and one untested mechanic, M zero three.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a design document. First, is the vision locked before the other sections are filled? If not, it is a Ghost Center.
Second, does every claim carry a tag, observed, inferred, missing or assumption, and did you open the cited line? A tag is a claim, not evidence.
Third, does each PX goal link to a mechanic, and each mechanic to a test? A mechanic with no linked test is a gap.
Fourth, are no more than forty percent of the features tagged CORE? More than that is priority inflation, and nothing is really core.
Fifth, does the out-of-scope list say what will not be built? A written list gives scope creep something to be measured against.
Sixth, could a stranger test each criterion, with a unit, a limit and a time box? Then say it exactly. Not make it complete, but every claim tagged, every test linked.

recap_lines: A brief agrees the task, and a GDD is detailed enough to build and test.
Reverse starts from a game, and a draft starts from an idea.
A PX goal is what the player feels, a mechanic what the player does.
Every claim carries a tag, and a tag is a claim, not evidence.
Priority Inflation means more than forty percent of features tagged CORE.
An acceptance criterion names a quantity, a tolerance and a time box.

your_turn.segment: Name The Design Term, Defend It
your_turn.command: Quiz me on game design document terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use reverse, draft, game brief, PX goal, mechanic, observed, assumption, scope creep, out of scope and acceptance criterion. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 14 step 3: the exact instruction 'Return the player within 0.2 m of the respawn point within 2 frames at --fixed-fps 60' and its measured 0.0898 m are criterion 5, which Chapter 5 labels a constructed fixture (a direct state write after activation, below y = −12). The instruction leaves out how the state is reached and the activation, which slide 11 step 1 says every criterion must name and slide 12 step 1 is about.

Slide 11 step 1, row 6 'old probes pass, 4 ≥ 4 checks' counts only input_probe.gd's four checks. Chapter 5's criterion 6 also requires feature_route.gd to still collect a coin, and slide 12 step 2 lists five old probes including 'a coin collected'. The two slides count the same invariants differently.
Slide 6 steps 1 to 3 and slide 14 step 1: 64%, 17% and 18% add to 99% (rounding of 107, 29 and 30 of 166). Correct, but a viewer may think a claim is unaccounted for.
Slide 11 step 3: the '0.0882 m: pass' label starts on the dashed 0.2 m ring, so its first digit sits on the line.

Badges do not match their contents: slide 12 is 'Illustrative data' but step 3's 21, 19 and 2 are real numbers from the Chapter 12 audio session (its own caption says so); slide 8 is 'Computed' but step 2 is captioned 'Illustrative arithmetic'.

Slide 7 step 2 (Mechanic Mirage) and slide 9 step 1 (Novelist's Trap): the TELL THESE APART box shows a pair that does not include the term just introduced (Ghost Center vs Implementation Void; Completeness Fallacy vs Stagnant Artifact), so the new term gets no look-alike.
Slide 13 pair 1: 'tags: OBSERVED' for reverse simplifies; a reverse also writes INFERRED and MISSING tags (slide 3 step 1 shows 29 and 30).

Slide 9 step 2: 'D-02 layer names, no reason recorded' reuses the ID of Chapter 5's real clawd decision D-02, which was a confident wrong decision with a stated reason, not a missing one. The table is labelled illustrative, but the shared ID may confuse.

Term names vary: the map says 'observed, inferred, missing, assumption' and 'cut/defer/swap' where the slides say '[OBSERVED]' and 'Cut, defer, swap'; the course glossary says 'Brief' and 'Out-of-scope list' where the slides say 'Game brief' and 'Out of scope'.
